Date Reported: [redacted date]

CLINICAL INFORMATION
Reason for Referral: Suspected adenocarcinoma of caecum requiring MSI testing
Clinical History: Elderly female patient with adenocarcinoma of caecum. Patient meets BETHESDA criteria for Lynch Syndrome testing.

SPECIMEN INFORMATION
Specimen Type 1: Tumor tissue from right hemicolectomy
Tumor Content: 80% neoplastic cells
Specimen Type 2: Peripheral blood

TEST PERFORMED
Microsatellite Instability (MSI) Analysis by PCR

METHODOLOGY
Microsatellite instability testing was attempted using the GeneTech MSI Analysis System. This assay employs multiplex PCR amplification of five quasi-monomorphic mononucleotide repeat markers: BAT-25, BAT-26, NR-21, NR-24, and MONO-27. These markers are highly sensitive for the detection of microsatellite instability associated with defective DNA mismatch repair.

The assay protocol involves:
- DNA extraction from both tumor tissue and matched normal blood sample
- PCR amplification using fluorescently labeled primers
- Capillary electrophoresis for fragment analysis
- Comparison of allelic patterns between tumor and normal DNA

MSI-High is defined as instability in ≥2 of the 5 markers
MSI-Low is defined as instability in 1 of the 5 markers
MSS (Microsatellite Stable) is defined as no instability detected

RESULTS
TEST FAILED - TECHNICAL FAILURE

Despite multiple attempts, PCR amplification failed for all five microsatellite markers in both the tumor tissue and blood samples:
- BAT-25: No amplification
- BAT-26: No amplification
- NR-21: No amplification
- NR-24: No amplification
- MONO-27: No amplification

Quality control markers also failed to amplify, indicating inadequate DNA quality or quantity for analysis.

INTERPRETATION
Microsatellite instability status could not be determined due to technical failure. The DNA extracted from both tumor and blood samples failed to amplify during PCR, preventing assessment of microsatellite stability. This technical failure impacts the ability to evaluate for Lynch Syndrome through MSI testing.

TECHNICAL NOTES
Possible causes of amplification failure include:
- DNA degradation due to formalin fixation or storage conditions
- Presence of PCR inhibitors
- Insufficient DNA quantity despite spectrophotometric measurements

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The inability to determine MSI status limits the molecular evaluation for Lynch Syndrome in this patient. MSI testing is a critical component in the screening algorithm for hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch Syndrome). Without this information, clinical management decisions regarding genetic counseling, germline testing, and family screening cannot be fully informed by MSI status.

LIMITATIONS
This test cannot detect all causes of Lynch Syndrome. Approximately 10-15% of Lynch Syndrome cases may have normal MSI status. Additionally, technical failures as encountered in this case prevent any determination of MSI status.
